summary:
A.R.E.S (Advanced Regolith & Environmental Survivor)6
Existing Mars maps answer "what is this place?" A.R.E.S answers a narrower question: "can the astronaut walk this route and get back?"
details:
A.R.E.S (Advanced Regolith & Environmental Survivor) plans a walking route
between two points on Mars and reports whether a suited astronaut can complete
it and return. The operator picks a start and a destination inside a 5.9 by
4.7 km working box on the northwest flank of Mount Sharp in Gale Crater. The
route recalculates in under 300 ms and returns walk time, distance, ascent and
descent, maximum slope, modelled surface temperature, radiation dose, remaining
EVA budget, the estimated point of no return, and a thermal advisory for any
stretch of ground that is unusually cold.

Five kinds of NASA data sit on one 4 m pixel grid: a 1 m digital elevation
model (topographic), CTX imagery at about 5 m (optical), the THEMIS daytime
infrared mosaic at 100 m (thermal), REMS weather for sol 4995 (atmospheric),
and the RAD background dose rate (radiation). A sixth layer, surface
temperature, is modelled from terrain geometry and is labelled as modelled
wherever it appears.

HOW IT WORKS
Elevation becomes slope and roughness, which become an 8-bit traversal cost
raster, with anything above 25 degrees marked impassable. A weighted A* search
with an octile heuristic finds the cheapest path across that grid. Walking time
is then derived along the finished path from a suited speed of 1.2 m/s, derated
by grade and by surface roughness. Dose is the RAD rate multiplied by duration.
The point of no return is the farthest point from which the budget still covers
the return.

The application is static files. No server, no build step, and no network
connection once the page has loaded, because Mars is 4 to 24 light-minutes away
and a crew cannot call home for help.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT
Existing tools such as Mars Trek are built for regional and global views.
A.R.E.S works at the scale of one walk, where a route is 2 to 5 km and the
binding constraint is not distance but time, air, and the return trip. It treats
the return as a first-class constraint, something a rover never has to consider.
The method is not specific to this site: any location with a digital elevation
model can be planned the same way.

TOOLS
Python 3 with rasterio, pyproj, numpy, scipy and Pillow for the data pipeline.
Plain JavaScript ES modules and a canvas for the interface, with A* written from
first principles rather than taken from a routing library. No framework and no
bundler. It runs on any laptop or tablet with a modern browser. Generative AI
assistants were used for code drafting and documentation, and are declared
separately in the submission form.

WHAT IS CREATIVE
Three things. First, the point of no return: the return trip is shown as a
visible constraint, so the EVA budget becomes spatial rather than abstract.
Second, the thermal advisory is expressed relative to the coldest decile of the
terrain instead of against an invented suit temperature limit, because there is
no defensible absolute limit available to cite. Third, every number on screen is
labelled as measured, derived or modelled, so a crew can see which values rest
on data and which rest on assumptions.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED
Safety first: radiation dose, cold ground, and terrain a suit cannot cross. That
the astronaut wears a suit and carries equipment, and therefore moves more
slowly than gravity alone would suggest. That light-time delay rules out live
support. And honesty about the data, including its resolutions, its mosaic
artefacts and the limits of a 4 m grid.

We also had the render reviewed. A mentor noticed that the leftmost fifth of the
map repeated the terrain beside it. We traced it to a misplaced block in the
source CTX mosaic, checked that the elevation model was unaffected, moved the
working box 1.3 km east, and recorded the finding in our methodology.
